judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 25B-1001. The federal government lets some business owners deduct part of their income before tax. Colorado has made high earners add that amount back when they figure their state tax. The rule was set to end after 2025, and the act makes it permanent. It applies to single filers above $500,000 and couples above $1 million. Farmers do not have to add the amount back. The Colorado House passed it 43-19 in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 25B-1002. Some corporations move profits to other countries to cut their Colorado tax. The state keeps a list of places it presumes are used that way. The act adds Hong Kong, Ireland, Liechtenstein, the Netherlands and Singapore to the list. From 2026 it also makes corporations add a federal break for foreign income back into the income Colorado taxes. The state tax chief can now rule on their own that a company is abroad for real business reasons. The Colorado House passed it 43-20 in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 25B-1003. Insurers with a home office in Colorado paid a 1 percent tax on the premiums they take in. Other insurers paid 2 percent. The act ends the lower rate in 2026, so every insurer pays 2 percent. The state auditor found that 15 of the 18 insurers taking the break cut about 4,300 Colorado jobs, while their tax saving grew by about $17.5 million. The Colorado House passed it 41-21 in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's changes to House Bill 25B-1006 and pass it. Federal money had been holding down the price of health plans that people buy on their own. That help was set to end after 2025. If Congress does not renew it, the act puts $100 million into a state fund. The state raises the money by selling tax credits to companies, and covers any gap from the general fund. The fund lowers what those buyers pay each month, and some of their other costs. The Colorado House voted 41-20 to accept those changes and pass the bill in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against accepting the Senate's changes to House Bill 25B-1006. Federal money had been holding down the price of health plans that people buy on their own. The Colorado House voted 41-20 to accept those changes and pass the bill in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.
judgments.note: Colorado votes twice to take the other chamber's changes: it concurs, then repasses the bill the same day. The acknowledged roll is that same-day concurrence vote, which precedes this repassage.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 25B-002. A federal law passed in July 2025 blocks Medicaid money from clinics that also do abortions. In Colorado that mainly means Planned Parenthood. The act tells the state to pay those clinics with state money instead. It covers Medicaid care given on or after July 1, 2025, such as exams, screening, birth control and infection care. It applies only when federal money cannot be used. Abortion care is left out, because Colorado already pays for that on its own. The Colorado Senate passed it 23-12 in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 25B-003. In November 2025 Colorado voters were asked to raise taxes on high earners to pay for free school meals. The act rewrites that ballot question. The money can now also go to food aid, the program known as SNAP. What is left after school meals can pay to run SNAP, help people apply, and teach about food. Lawmakers acted after a federal budget law cut SNAP and pushed costs onto the states. The Colorado Senate passed it 23-12 in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 25B-004. A 2024 Colorado law makes companies that build or use high-risk artificial intelligence guard against bias. They must also tell a person when such a system is deciding about them. Those duties were due to start on February 1, 2026. The act moves every one of those dates to June 30, 2026. It changes nothing else. The Colorado House passed it 48-14 in the August 2025 special session, and the governor signed it into law.
